title: Cooperative worker yield and parse throttle scratchpad
body:
Summary:
This is a working scratchpad for a cluster of small experiments exploring an under-observed CPU source of tail latency: frequent worker park/unpark and interpreter yielding during request-parse + tokenization on small payloads. Hypothesis is that for many 50-500B requests we pay a disproportionate amount of CPU to short-lived Python-side work (header parsing, JSON->dict allocation, tokenization entry/exit) plus the cost of thread handoffs and syscalls that follow each request boundary.

Why this matters:
- Small requests are the majority of traffic in some customers (PLG chatbots, completion calls from UI).
- Per-request cost multiplies with RPS; small inefficiencies lead to large billable CPU and tail latency.
- We already have batching + KV caching on the hot path, but parsing + tokenize still runs on the CPU worker before entering the model kernel.

What we ran (executables & env):
- Test harness: local harness that emulates nginx -> runtime worker queue used in prod (repo:runtimes/inproc-harness).
- Workload: synthetic 64B/128B/320B payload mixes, 1000 RPS sustained, 5s bursts to 10k RPS.
- Counters: perf, eBPF tracepoints for sched_wakeup/sched_switch, strace sampling for syscalls, Py-alloc sampling (tracemalloc), and flamegraphs from async-profiler.
- Hosts: c6i.8x-like CPU shape for baseline; separate run on n2-highcpu for comparison.

Key observations:
1) Park/unpark counts scale linearly with RPS for small requests. Each request lifecycle shows ~2-4 wakeups per worker: accept -> parse -> handoff -> tokenizer -> dispatch. wakeup latency (time between sched_wakeup and the subsequent sched_switch where the target runs) has a long tail (up to 2ms) on noisy nodes.
2) Syscall profile: a surprising number of short-lived syscalls are visible during parse: readv on socket, getrandom (tokenizer seeding for some libs), writev for tracing headers, multiple futex wake/futex wait pairs from small locks in Python C extensions.
3) Tokenization boundary costs: entry/exit overhead of the tokenizer C extension is small relative to pure-Python JSON decoding, but when combined with PyObject allocations it dominates for "few-token" requests.
4) JSON parse allocations: constructing dicts and small strings accounts for ~35-50% of pre-kernel CPU for the smallest payloads in our harness. reusing a C-backed small parser reduces this by ~25% in microbenchmarks.
5) GIL contention is visible but not the dominant contributor; rather, the combined effect of interpreter context switches and short critical sections (C-extension locks, refcount updates) causes more latencies.

Dug-in experiments and results:
- Experiment: cooperative-yield shim (pyshim) that yields the interpreter less aggressively and batches parse work per-thread. Result: tail latency improved by ~18% on 64B payloads but increased average memory live set due to pooled dict reuse.
- Experiment: offload header parsing to a small Rust binary via inproc socket (shared mem) that returns a compact token list instead of dict. Result: CPU pre-kernel reduced by 28% for 128B requests, park/unpark events fell ~20% because the Rust parser performs fewer syscalls and uses fewer short locks.
- Experiment: replace CPython json.loads with simdjson C binding. Result: 40% improvement in parse throughput but introduced a small allocation pattern mismatch that required a conversion layer; net win still positive.
- Experiment: threadpool tweak to keep a warm pool of pinned tokenizer threads (affinity pinned) that avoid park/unpark on frequent bursts. Result: 10-15% tail improvement in noisy machines; cost is more complex scheduling and potential unfairness for long-running requests.

Open hypothesis to validate:
- Are many wakeups coming from internal tracing/log hooks? We saw writev calls for audit/tracing that trigger additional scheduling activity. One run with tracing disabled cut wakeups by ~12%. Need to validate across customers.
- Would a lock-free single-writer queue between acceptor and tokenizer reduce futex churn? Quick microbench for MPSC ring shows promise in synthetic tests.

Actionable next steps (short-term):
- Create an A/B perf test in dedicated infra to validate Rust header-parser across real traffic (INF ticket: INF-998).
- Instrument tracing write path to gate heavy trace writes behind a sampling policy for small requests.
- Prototype a per-vCPU pinned tokenizer thread pool with warm handoff semantics; measure memory overhead and fairness.
- Add eBPF sampling to CI perf runs to correlate sched_wakeup latencies with noisy co-tenants.

Longer-term ideas:
- Native zero-copy request parsing: keep raw buffer in C, provide token iterator to Python layer to avoid repeated small string allocations.
- Move more lightweight parsing to a shared parse process (multi-tenant) that returns compact parse tokens over shared memory for low-sensitivity fields.
- Revisit subinterpreter experiments with a focus on reducing interpreter switching costs rather than GIL elimination. Prior notes (gil-subinterpreter-experiments) looked at correctness; we should re-evaluate for fast-path small requests.

Notes to self / open questions:
- Need a better way to quantify cost per wakeup (cpu-time attributable vs scheduling latency). perf stat + tracepoints gave signals but we need an accounting tool that attributes blocked time to wakeup events.
- Verify whether getrandom calls are from third-party libs (tokenizers) or internal; if the former, add PRs to lazy-seed RNGs.
- Check interaction with tls/session caches: do repeated small requests cause repeated session lookup work?

Tickets referenced / suggested:
- INF-987 (current sampling run)
- INF-998 (rust-header-parser AB test)
- PERF-212 (pinned-tokenizer prototype)

If you're reading this and want to try replicating: start with the inproc harness, payload mixes in harness/configs, run with perf + /sys/kernel/debug/tracing snapshots, and iterate on the small parser shim before changing threadpool semantics.

Small checklist for next meeting:
- [ ] Kick off INF-998 and allocate staging infra
- [ ] Disable tracing for a subset of hosts and compare wakeup counts
- [ ] Share pinned-tokenizer prototype with the team for feedback

This doc intentionally mixes raw notes, partial results, and TODOs — keep it as a working scratchpad until we lock the rust-parser AB test or the per-vCPU pinned pool prototype.
